evidence.field: A00046 了: Shuowen explanation and meanings
evidence.text: The entry reproduces the received Shuowen account 尦也。从子無臂，象形 (‘尦; from 子 without arms; pictograph’). It separately records a legs-crossing sense, early examples for clever/understanding, a Song example for understanding right from wrong, and later examples of ‘finish/end’. It also records the le particle in literary examples. These dictionary examples establish documented uses, but do not by themselves establish the earliest occurrence or a path between senses.
evidence.title: [A00046] 了 - Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.source: 汉典, character entry and Shuowen/Duan Yucai material
evidence.field: 字源字形; 说文解字; 说文解字注
evidence.text: The entry gives the received Shuowen explanation 尦也。从子無臂。象形 and Duan Yucai’s interpretation involving crossed lower legs and 了戾 (‘twisted/entangled’). The entry also reports borrowing for 憭悟. These are historical explanations, not direct confirmation of an early depicted referent or proof of how ‘finish’ came to be written with 了.

evidence.text: The article describes Tang–Song structures V-le, V-O-le, and V-le-O: lexical verb ‘finish’ develops resultative-complement uses, and Song examples of V-le-O mark perfective aspect. It reports post-Song V-O-le before sentence-final 也 as an anterior marker. This is a scholarly analysis of grammatical development; the inspected abstract supplies no dated primary quotations.
evidence.title: On Grammatical Functions and Meanings of the Verb ‘–Le’ in the Tang-Song Dynasties

search_audit.query: 了 finish Han dynasty attestation 了 讫也 毕也 earliest usage
search_audit.outcome: The official MOE entry reports uses and cited works for multiple senses. Chinese Text Project result surfaced historical dictionary text, but direct opening returned 403. No securely dated earliest lexical ‘finish’ attestation was established.

gaps: No securely dated earliest graphic attestation or primary inscription image was verified. The received Shuowen account is historical testimony, and the competing child-without-arms, crossed-legs, and entangled-legs readings remain unsettled.

The Commons seal-style image is a modern redraw of a received Shuowen form; it cannot adjudicate the disputed interpretations or establish an ancient graphic sequence. Its cited S10990 underlying data were not independently inspected.

No local or external evidence establishes an independently recoverable ancient name/pronunciation for a depicted object, so a sound-loan explanation of ‘finish’ remains unverified. The alternative entangled/twisted-to-tied-to-finished semantic chain lacks dated intermediate examples.

Historical dictionaries attest several senses, but their cited examples and ordering do not establish which sense came first. The relative chronology of understanding/cleverness and finishing remains open.

Tang–Song grammaticalization stages are supported by a scholarly abstract, but this pass did not inspect dated primary quotations. The exact earliest particle attestation and the later sentence-final development remain incompletely sourced.

Local primary reading rows were available for both 了 and 瞭 and are reported separately. The exact official Unicode pages were inaccessible; no claim of official-page verification is made. No Baxter–Sagart comparison is available in the supplied research context.

No phonetic component is identified in 了’s received Shuowen analysis. 瞭 is a separate related character with reported 目 semantic plus 尞 phonetic analysis in the dossier, but this pass did not retrieve exact local Baxter–Sagart rows for 尞 or 瞭 and does not use related readings to infer 了’s origin.
No bulk extract is recommended: the consulted material is character-specific, and no general reuse permission for a local corpus extract was verified.
